facts.text: Article 128 § 4 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides that any person arrested or whose police custody has been extended can challenge that measure before a judge to secure immediate release; this application may be lodged by the person or their lawyer, legal representative, close relatives or spouse.

facts.text: At the material time, there was no legislation governing the right of people in police custody to contact their families; the legislative amendment providing for notification of detainees’ families was enacted only in 2002.

anchor.surface_text: 37.  The Court reiterates that, at the material time, there was no legislation governing the right of people in police custody to contact their families or others, as the legislative amendment providing for the notification of detainees’ families was not enacted until 2002.

facts.text: Although the applicants could not prove they had been refused permission to contact their families, the procedure for arranging such contact had not been clearly established and the Government did not indicate what means were available to the applicants to make contact rapidly after being taken into custody.

anchor.surface_text: In the present case, although the applicants were unable to prove that they had been refused permission to contact their families, the procedure for arranging such contact had not been clearly established either. The Government, for their part, did not indicate what means had been available to the applicants to make contact with their families rapidly after being taken into custody.

issues.text: Whether the applicants exhausted domestic remedies under Article 128 § 4 of the Code of Criminal Procedure before complaining under Article 8 of the Convention

anchor.surface_text: The Government submitted that the applicants had not exhausted domestic remedies, referring to the remedy provided for under Article 128 § 4 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraph 18 above). They argued, in particular, that if the applicants had requested to make contact with their families they would not have been prevented from doing so.

issues.text: Whether the applicants' complaint under Article 8 of the Convention is justified given the lack of legislation governing the right of individuals in police custody to contact their families

anchor.surface_text: The Court considers, firstly, that the complaint in the present case is not that the State acted but that it failed to act. The situation stems from a lack of legislation governing the right of individuals in police custody to contact their families. The Court thus considers that it must examine the case in the light of the general rule contained in the first paragraph of Article 8 of the Convention, which lays down the right to respect for private and family life.

issues.text: Whether the State had positive obligations under Article 8 to ensure respect for family life by allowing detainees to contact their families

anchor.surface_text: In this connection, the Court would reaffirm the principle that has already been established in substance under Article 8: although the essential object of Article 8 is to protect the individual against arbitrary action by the public authorities, it does not merely compel the State to refrain from such interference, as there may in addition be positive obligations inherent in an effective “respect” for family life. Whilst the boundaries between the State’s positive and negative obligations under this provision do not lend themselves to precise definition, the applicable principles are nevertheless similar.

issues.text: Whether the incommunicado detention of the applicants for more than seven days without contact with their families violated Article 8 of the Convention

anchor.surface_text: The Court observes that it may be extremely important for a person who has been arrested to be able to communicate with his or her family promptly. The unexplained disappearance of a family member, even for a short period, may cause deep anxiety ... In the present case the Court observes that the applicants were held incommunicado for more than seven days, with all the anxiety which that entailed both for them and their families.

issues.text: Whether the absence of a legislative framework at the material time providing for notification of detainees’ families and contact rights constituted a violation of Article 8

anchor.surface_text: The Court reiterates that, at the material time, there was no legislation governing the right of people in police custody to contact their families or others, as the legislative amendment providing for the notification of detainees’ families was not enacted until 2002. In the present case, although the applicants were unable to prove that they had been refused permission to contact their families, the procedure for arranging such contact had not been clearly established either.
